author: deustp01
body: In humans, there are two different enzymes, encoded by two different genes. One consumes ammonia as a step in the urea cycle; the other consumes glutamine as a step in pyrimidine biosynthesis, so the human enzymes enable two mechanistically distinct molecular functions that are parts of two different processes. Yeasts can synthesize pyrimidines de novo; no clue what they do with urea.

author: ValWood
body:
we (yeast) have 2 separate enzymes too for pyrimidine biosynthesis and urea, but currently both enzymes are annotated to both terms from various sources ....

Also if my initial comment is correct, 
human is incorrect via this mapping too
https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P27708/entry#function

author: deustp01
body: The human biochemistry is that there is normally no cross-talk - product of the (ammonia) enzyme feeds only urea biosynthesis and product of the (glutamine) enzyme feeds only pyrimidine biosynthesis. There is disease cross-talk: individuals with a defect in later steps of urea synthesis also synthesize abnormally high levels of pyrimidines, driven by the availability of excess carbamoyl phosphate. Again no clue about normal versus pathological states in yeast.

author: ValWood
body: I would expect no cross-talk here because pyrimidine biosynthesis in the cytosol and the urea pathway (at least this part) is in the mitochondria.

author: deustp01
body: Exactly. None under normal conditions. If a downstream mutation blocks the utilization of carbamoyl phosphate for urea synthesis then the accumulated excess can spill over into the other process.

author: sjm41
body:
I took a look at this, focussing on annotations to human, fly and the two yeasts.

In terms of genes, looks like fly is the odd one out with only a single ortholog encoding these related enzymes:
- human: CPS1 & CAD
- fly: rudimentary (CG18572) 
- cerevisiae CPA2 & URA2
- pombe: arg4 & ura1

---

Definition of GO:0004087/EC:6.3.4.16:

id: GO:0004087
name: carbamoyl-phosphate synthase (ammonia) activity
def: "Catalysis of the reaction: 2 ATP + hydrogencarbonate + NH4+ = 2 ADP + carbamoyl phosphate + 2 H+ + phosphate." [EC:6.3.4.16, RHEA:18029]
xref: EC:6.3.4.16
xref: KEGG_REACTION:R00149
xref: MetaCyc:RXN-13202
xref: RHEA:18029
is_a: GO:0016879 ! ligase activity, forming carbon-nitrogen bonds

EC:6.3.4.16 entry says:
- The enzyme catalyzes the first committed step in the **urea cycle**.
- The reaction proceeds via three separate chemical reactions: phosphorylation of hydrogencarbonate to carboxyphosphate; a nucleophilic attack of ammonia on carboxyphosphate yielding carbamate; and the phosphorylation of carbamate forming carbamoyl phosphate.
- Two moles of ATP are utilized for the synthesis of one molecule of carbamoyl phosphate, making the reaction essentially irreversible.
- The enzyme requires the allosteric activator N-acetyl-L-glutamate.
- cf. EC [6.3.5.5](https://enzyme.expasy.org/EC/6.3.5.5).

Wikipedia entry (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbamoyl_phosphate_synthetase_I):
- referred to as "Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I"
- says this is "located in the [mitochondria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitochondria) involved in the production of [urea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urea). Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS1 or CPSI) transfers an [ammonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonia) molecule to a molecule of [bicarbonate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicarbonate) that has been phosphorylated by a molecule of ATP. The resulting [carbamate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbamate) is then phosphorylated with another molecule of ATP."

---

Definition of GO:0004088/EC:6.3.5.5:

id: GO:0004088
name: carbamoyl-phosphate synthase (glutamine-hydrolyzing) activity
def: "Catalysis of the reaction: 2 ATP + L-glutamine + CO2 + H2O = 2 ADP + phosphate + glutamate + carbamoyl phosphate." [EC:6.3.5.5, RHEA:18633]
xref: EC:6.3.5.5
xref: MetaCyc:CARBPSYN-RXN
xref: RHEA:18633
is_a: GO:0016884 ! carbon-nitrogen ligase activity, with glutamine as amido-N-donor

NOTE: the GO def needs updating to "hydrogencarbonate + L-glutamine + 2 ATP + H2O = carbamoyl phosphate + L-glutamate + 2 ADP + phosphate + 2 H+" to match RHEA/EC (see https://github.com/geneontology/go-ontology/issues/30008)

EC:6.3.5.5 entry says:
- The product carbamoyl phosphate is an intermediate in the **biosynthesis of arginine and the pyrimidine nucleotides**.
- The enzyme from Escherichia coli has three separate active sites, which are connected by a molecular tunnel that is almost 100 A in length.
- The amidotransferase domain within the small subunit of the enzyme hydrolyzes glutamine to ammonia via a thioester intermediate.
- The ammonia migrates through the interior of the protein, where it reacts with carboxyphosphate to produce the carbamate intermediate.
- The carboxyphosphate intermediate is formed by the phosphorylation of hydrogencarbonate by ATP at a site contained within the N-terminal half of the large subunit.
- The carbamate intermediate is transported through the interior of the protein to a second site within the C-terminal half of the large subunit, where it is phosphorylated by another ATP to yield the final product, carbamoyl phosphate.
- cf. EC [6.3.4.16](https://enzyme.expasy.org/EC/6.3.4.16).


Wikipedia entry (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbamoyl_phosphate_synthase_II):
- referred to as "Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II"
- says "is an enzyme that catalyzes the reactions that produce [carbamoyl phosphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbamoyl_phosphate) in the [cytosol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cytosol) (as opposed to type I, which functions in the [mitochondria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitochondria))....It is one of the four functional enzymatic domains coded by the [CAD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CAD_(gene)) gene.

---

Annotations to GO:0004087/EC:6.3.4.16:

EXP GO annotations to:
- human CPS1
- (no fly/yeast EXP annotations)

EC:6.3.4.16 annotated in Swiss-Prot to:
- human CPS1 (from 2 publications) and CAD (ISS from S. cerevisiae URA2)
- fly rudimentary (CG18572) ISS from (ISS from S. cerevisiae URA2)
- S. cerevisiae CPA2 (3 publications) and URA2 (3 publications)
- S. pombe ura1 (1 publication) and arg4 (ISS from Q7SH52)

---

Annotations to GO:0004088/EC:6.3.5.5:

EXP GO annotations to:
- (no human EXP annotations, but several mouse & rat annotations to CAD orthologs)
- fly rudimentary (CG18572)
- cerevisiae CPA1, CPA2 and URA2
- pombe ura1

EC:6.3.5.5 annotated in Swiss-Prot to:
- human CAD (P27708)
- fly rudimentary (CG18572) from 1 publication
- S. cerevisiae CPA1, CPA2 and URA2
- S. pombe arg4, arg5 and ura1

---

So, based on this (and not having researched any further), it seems:

- human CPS1 => GO:0004087/EC:6.3.4.16 (mito)
- human CAD => GO:0004088/EC:6.3.5.5 (cyto)

- fly rudimentary (CG18572) => GO:0004088/EC:6.3.5.5 (cyto) ONLY

- S. cerevisiae CPA2 => ?? (needs more research)
- S. cerevisiae URA2 => ??  (needs more research)

- S. pombe arg4 => GO:0004087/EC:6.3.4.16 (mito)
- S. pombe ura1 => GO:0004088/EC:6.3.5.5 (cyto)

author: sjm41
body:
ChatGPT explains why Drosophila is the odd one out (from the species looked at above):

Q) does drosophila have a 'carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I' (CPS1) enzyme?

No, Drosophila does not have a carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS1) enzyme. CPS1 is a mitochondrial enzyme found in vertebrates, where it plays a crucial role in the urea cycle, converting ammonia and bicarbonate into carbamoyl phosphate.

However, Drosophila does have a carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPSII) enzyme, which is part of a bifunctional CAD protein involved in pyrimidine biosynthesis. Unlike CPS1, CPSII operates in the cytoplasm and uses glutamine rather than ammonia as the nitrogen donor.

Since insects like Drosophila do not have a urea cycle, they do not require CPS1. Instead, they primarily excrete nitrogenous waste as uric acid (uricotelic excretion).
